title: Book 3, Chapter 11 — Year of the War—Campaigns of Demosthenes in Western Greece—Ruin of Ambracia
paragraphs: Summer was now over. In the winter that followed, the plague attacked the Athenians a second time. It had never entirely left them, but its ravages had notably abated. This second visit lasted no less than a year, whereas the first had lasted two, and nothing distressed the Athenians and reduced their power more than this. No fewer than four thousand four hundred heavy infantry in the ranks died of it, and three hundred cavalry, besides a number of the common people that was never ascertained. At the same time came the many earthquakes at Athens, in Euboea and in Boeotia, particularly at Orchomenus in Boeotia.

That same winter the Athenians in Sicily, with the Rhegians, sailed against the islands of Aeolus with thirty ships. In summer an invasion was impossible there, because the islands lack water. The Liparaeans, a Cnidian colony, hold them. They live on Lipara, one of the group and not a large island, and from it they farm the others: Didyme, Strongyle and Hiera. The people of those parts believe that Hephaestus has his forge in Hiera, because they see it throw up a great deal of flame by night and smoke by day. The islands lie off the coast of the Sicels and the Messinese, and were allies of the Syracusans. The Athenians ravaged their land. The inhabitants would not submit, and the Athenians sailed back to Rhegium. So the winter ended, and with it the fifth year of this war, of which Thucydides was the historian.

The next summer the Peloponnesians and their allies set out to invade Attica under Agis, son of Archidamus. They went as far as the Isthmus, but there were numerous earthquakes, and they turned back without the invasion taking place. At about the time when these earthquakes were so common, the sea at Orobiae, in Euboea, drew back from the line of coast as it then was, and returned in a huge wave. It flooded a great part of the town and retreated, leaving some of it still under water. So what was once land is now sea, and those of the inhabitants who could not run up to higher ground in time perished. A similar flood occurred at Atalanta, the island off the coast of the Opuntian Locrians. It carried away part of the Athenian fort and wrecked one of two ships that had been drawn up on the beach. At Peparethus the sea also drew back a little, though no flood followed, and an earthquake threw down part of the wall, the town hall and a few other buildings. The cause of this phenomenon, in my opinion, must be sought in the earthquake. Where its shock has been most violent, the sea is driven back and then suddenly recoils with redoubled force, and this causes the flood. Without an earthquake I do not see how such an accident could happen.

During the same summer the different belligerents carried on different operations in Sicily: the Siceliots against each other, and the Athenians and their allies. I shall, however, confine myself to the actions in which the Athenians took part, choosing the most important. The Athenian general Charoeades was killed in battle by the Syracusans, and this left Laches in sole command of the fleet. He now led it, together with the allies, against Mylae, a place belonging to the Messinese. Two Messinese battalions were garrisoned at Mylae, and they laid an ambush for the party landing from the ships. The Athenians and their allies routed them with great slaughter, then assaulted the fortification and forced them to surrender the Acropolis and march with them against Messina. This town also submitted afterwards, when the Athenians and their allies approached, and gave hostages and all the other securities demanded.

The same summer the Athenians sent thirty ships around Peloponnese under Demosthenes, son of Alcisthenes, and Procles, son of Theodorus. They sent sixty other ships, with two thousand heavy infantry, under Nicias, son of Niceratus, against Melos, wishing to reduce the Melians, who, although islanders, refused to be subjects of Athens or even to join her confederacy. The devastation of their land did not win their submission, so the fleet weighed anchor from Melos and sailed to Oropus in the territory of Graea. Landing at nightfall, the heavy infantry set out at once from the ships by land for Tanagra in Boeotia. There they were met, at a signal agreed beforehand, by the whole levy from Athens under Hipponicus, son of Callias, and Eurymedon, son of Thucles. They encamped and spent that day ravaging the Tanagraean territory, and stayed there for the night. The next day they defeated those Tanagraeans who sailed out against them, together with some Thebans who had come up to help the Tanagraeans. They took some arms, set up a trophy, and withdrew, the troops to the city and the others to the ships. Nicias with his sixty ships coasted along the shore, ravaged the Locrian seaboard, and so returned home.

About this time the Lacedaemonians founded their colony of Heraclea in Trachis, for the following reason. The Malians form three tribes in all: the Paralians, the Hiereans and the Trachinians. The Trachinians had suffered severely in a war with their neighbors the Oetaeans, and at first intended to give themselves up to Athens. Then they feared that they would not find in her the security they sought, and sent to Lacedaemon, having chosen Tisamenus as their ambassador. The Dorians from the mother country of the Lacedaemonians joined in this embassy with the same request, since they suffered from the same enemy. After hearing them, the Lacedaemonians determined to send out the colony. They wished to assist the Trachinians and Dorians, and they also thought that the proposed town would lie conveniently for the war against the Athenians. A fleet could be made ready there against Euboea, with the advantage of a short passage to the island, and the town would also be useful as a station on the road to Thrace. In short, everything made the Lacedaemonians eager to found the place. They first consulted the god at Delphi and received a favorable answer. Then they sent off the colonists, Spartans and Perioeci, and invited any others of the Hellenes who wished to go with them, except Ionians, Achaeans and certain other nationalities. Three Lacedaemonians led them as founders of the colony: Leon, Alcidas and Damagon. Once the settlement was made, they fortified the city anew. It is now called Heraclea, and lies about four miles and a half from Thermopylae and two miles and a quarter from the sea. They began building docks, and closed the side toward Thermopylae right at the pass itself, so that the place could be easily defended.

The foundation of this town was evidently meant to annoy Euboea, since the passage across to Cenaeum in that island is a short one. At first it caused some alarm at Athens, which the event, however, did nothing to justify, for the town never gave the Athenians any trouble. The reason was as follows. The Thessalians were sovereign in those parts, and their territory was menaced by the foundation of the town. They were afraid that it might prove a very powerful neighbor, and so they continually harassed and made war on the new settlers, until they wore them out, in spite of their originally considerable numbers, since people flocked from all quarters to a place founded by the Lacedaemonians and therefore thought secure of prosperity. On the other hand, the Lacedaemonians themselves, in the persons of their governors, did their full share toward ruining its prosperity and reducing its population. They frightened away the greater part of the inhabitants by governing harshly and in some cases unfairly, and so made it easier for their neighbors to prevail against them.

The same summer, at about the time when the Athenians were detained at Melos, their fellow citizens in the thirty ships cruising around Peloponnese cut off some guards in an ambush at Ellomenus in Leucadia. They then went against Leucas itself with a large armament, having been reinforced by the whole levy of the Acarnanians except Oeniadae, and by the Zacynthians, the Cephallenians and fifteen ships from Corcyra. The Leucadians watched their land being devastated, both outside and inside the isthmus on which the town of Leucas and the temple of Apollo stand, but made no move because of the overwhelming numbers of the enemy. The Acarnanians urged Demosthenes, the Athenian general, to build a wall to cut the town off from the continent. They were convinced that this measure would secure its capture and rid them once and for all of a most troublesome enemy.

Meanwhile the Messenians had persuaded Demosthenes that he had a fine opportunity. With so large an army gathered, he should attack the Aetolians. They were enemies of Naupactus, and reducing them would also make it easy to bring the rest of that part of the continent over to Athens. The Aetolians were a numerous and warlike nation, but they lived in unwalled villages far apart from one another and had only light armor. The Messenians said they could be subdued without much difficulty before any help could reach them. They recommended attacking the Apodotians first, then the Ophionians, and after them the Eurytanians. These are the largest tribe in Aetolia; their language is said to be exceedingly hard to understand, and they eat their meat raw. When these were subdued, the rest would easily submit.

Demosthenes consented to this plan, not only to please the Messenians, but also in the belief that by adding the Aetolians to his other continental allies he would be able to march against the Boeotians without aid from home. He would go by way of Ozolian Locris to Kytinium in Doris, keeping Parnassus on his right until he descended to the Phocians. These he could force to join him if their ancient friendship for Athens did not, as he expected, decide them at once. Once in Phocis he would already be on the frontier of Boeotia. He therefore weighed anchor from Leucas, against the wish of the Acarnanians, and sailed with his whole armament along the coast to Sollium, where he told them his intention. They refused to agree to it because Leucas was not being besieged, so he started on his expedition against the Aetolians with the rest of the forces: the Cephallenians, the Messenians and the Zacynthians, and three hundred Athenian marines from his own ships (the fifteen Corcyraean vessels had departed). He established his base at Oeneon in Locris, since the Ozolian Locrians were allies of Athens and were to meet him with all their forces in the interior. They were neighbors of the Aetolians and armed in the same way, and it was thought that their knowledge of the country and of the enemy’s manner of fighting would make them of great service on the expedition.

Demosthenes bivouacked with the army in the precinct of Nemean Zeus, where the poet Hesiod is said to have been killed by the people of the country, in accordance with an oracle that had foretold he would die in Nemea. At daybreak he set out to invade Aetolia. The first day he took Potidania, the next Krokyle, and the third Tichium, where he halted and sent the booty back to Eupalium in Locris. He had determined to pursue his conquests as far as the Ophionians, and, if they refused to submit, to return to Naupactus and make them the object of a second expedition. Meanwhile the Aetolians had known of his design from the moment it was formed. As soon as the army invaded their country, they came up in great force with all their tribes. Even the most remote Ophionians, the Bomiensians and the Calliensians, who extend toward the Malian Gulf, were among them.

The Messenians, however, stood by their original advice. They assured Demosthenes that the Aetolians were an easy conquest. He should press on as fast as he could, they said, and try to take each village as he came to it, instead of waiting until the whole nation was under arms against him. His advisers led him on, and he trusted in his fortune, since nobody had opposed him so far. He did not wait for the Locrian reinforcements, who were to have supplied the light-armed darters he lacked most. He advanced and stormed Aegitium. Its inhabitants fled before him and took positions on the hills above the town, which stood on high ground about nine miles from the sea. By now the Aetolians had gathered to the rescue. They attacked the Athenians and their allies, running down from the hills on every side and hurling javelins. When the Athenian army advanced they fell back, and when it retired they came on. For a long time the battle went this way, with advance and retreat in turn, and in both the Athenians had the worst.

Still, as long as their archers had arrows left and could use them, the Athenians held out, and the light-armed Aetolians retired before the arrows. But the captain of the archers was killed and his men were scattered. The soldiers, wearied by the constant repetition of the same exertions and hard pressed by the Aetolian javelins, at last turned and fled. They fell into pathless gullies and places they did not know, and so perished, for the Messenian Chromon, their guide, had also unfortunately been killed. A great many were overtaken in the pursuit by the swift-footed, light-armed Aetolians and fell beneath their javelins. The greater number, however, missed their road and rushed into a wood that had no way out, and the enemy soon set it on fire and burned it around them. Indeed the Athenian army fell victim to death in every form and suffered every vicissitude of flight. The survivors escaped with difficulty to the sea and to Oeneon in Locris, from which they had set out. Many of the allies were killed, and about one hundred and twenty Athenian heavy infantry, not a man less, and all in the prime of life. These were by far the best men of the city of Athens to fall during this war. Among the slain was also Procles, the colleague of Demosthenes. The Athenians took up their dead from the Aetolians under truce, withdrew to Naupactus, and from there went in their ships to Athens. Demosthenes stayed behind in Naupactus and its neighborhood, afraid to face the Athenians after the disaster.
At about the same time the Athenians on the coast of Sicily sailed to Locris. They landed from their ships, defeated the Locrians who came out against them, and captured a fort on the river Halex.

The same summer the Aetolians had sent an embassy to Corinth and Lacedaemon before the Athenian expedition. It consisted of Tolophus, an Ophionian, Boriades, an Eurytanian, and Tisander, an Apodotian. They now obtained the dispatch of an army to help them against Naupactus, which had invited the Athenian invasion. Toward autumn the Lacedaemonians sent out three thousand heavy infantry of the allies, five hundred of them from Heraclea, the newly founded city in Trachis. Eurylochus, a Spartan, commanded them, with Macarius and Menedaius, also Spartans, at his side.

The army assembled at Delphi, and Eurylochus sent a herald to the Ozolian Locrians. The road to Naupactus ran through their territory, and he also had in mind to detach them from Athens. In Locris his chief supporters were the Amphissians, who were alarmed by the hostility of the Phocians. They were the first to give hostages, and for fear of the invading army they induced the rest to do likewise. The first were their neighbors the Myonians, who held the most difficult of the passes. After them came the Ipnians, Messapians, Tritaeans, Chalaeans, Tolophonians, Hessians and Oeanthians, who all joined in the expedition. The Olpaeans gave hostages but did not accompany the invasion. The Hyaeans refused both, until Polis, one of their villages, was captured.

When his preparations were finished, Eurylochus lodged the hostages in Kytinium, in Doris, and advanced on Naupactus through Locrian country. Two Locrian towns, Oeneon and Eupalium, refused to join him, and he took them on the way. In the territory of Naupactus the Aetolians joined him. The army laid waste the land and took the suburb of the town, which had no walls, and then also Molycrium, a Corinthian colony subject to Athens. Meanwhile the Athenian Demosthenes had stayed near Naupactus since the affair in Aetolia. He heard of the army and feared for the town, so he went to the Acarnanians and persuaded them to relieve it, though not without difficulty, because he had left Leucas. They sent a thousand heavy infantry with him on his ships. These threw themselves into the place and saved it, for the length of its wall and the small number of its defenders would otherwise have put it in the gravest danger. Eurylochus and his companions found that this force had gone in and that storming the town was impossible. They withdrew, not to Peloponnese, but to the country once called Aeolis, now Calydon and Pleuron, to the places around it, and to Proschium in Aetolia. The Ambraciots had come and urged them to join in attacking Amphilochian Argos and the rest of Amphilochia and Acarnania. They affirmed that conquering these countries would bring the whole continent into alliance with Lacedaemon. Eurylochus agreed and dismissed the Aetolians. With his army he stayed quietly in those parts until the Ambraciots should take the field and he could join them before Argos.

Summer was now over. In the winter that followed, the Athenians in Sicily marched with their Hellenic allies against the Sicel town of Inessa, whose acropolis was held by the Syracusans. They were joined by those Sicels, subjects or allies of Syracuse, who had revolted from her and come over to their army. They attacked Inessa without being able to take it, and retired. During the retreat, the allies who were retreating behind the Athenians were attacked by the Syracusans from the fort, and a large part of their army was routed with great slaughter. After this, Laches and the Athenians from the ships made some descents on Locris. They defeated the Locrians, who came against them under Proxenus, son of Capaton, on the river Caicinus, took some arms and departed.

That same winter the Athenians purified Delos, it appears in obedience to a certain oracle. Pisistratus the tyrant had purified it before, though not the whole island, only the part visible from the temple. Now the whole island was purified, in this manner. They dug up all the graves of those who had died on Delos, and ordered that from then on nobody might die or give birth on the island. The dying and the women in labor were to be carried across to Rhenea. Rhenea lies so close to Delos that Polycrates, tyrant of Samos, dedicated it to the Delian Apollo by binding it to Delos with a chain, after he had added it to his other island conquests in the period of his naval ascendancy.

After the purification, the Athenians celebrated for the first time the Delian games, which are held every fifth year. In ancient times, indeed, there had been a great assembly of the Ionians and the neighboring islanders at Delos. They used to come to the festival, as the Ionians now do to that of Ephesus, and athletic and poetic contests took place there, and the cities brought choirs of dancers. Nothing is clearer on this point than the following verses of Homer, from a hymn to Apollo:

Phœbus, wherever you stray, far or near, Delos was still of all your haunts most dear. Thither the robed Ionians take their way With wife and child to keep your holiday, Invoke your favor on each manly game, And dance and sing in honor of your name.

That there was also a poetic contest, in which the Ionians went to compete, is again shown by the following verses from the same hymn. After celebrating the Delian dance of the women, he ends his song of praise with these verses, in which he also alludes to himself:

Well, may Apollo keep you all! and so, Sweethearts, good-bye — yet tell me not I go Out from your hearts; and if in after hours Some other wanderer in this world of ours Touch at your shores, and ask your maidens here Who sings the songs the sweetest to your ear, Think of me then, and answer with a smile, ‘A blind old man of Scio’s rocky isle.’

Homer thus attests that there was anciently a great assembly and festival at Delos. In later times the islanders and the Athenians continued to send choirs of dancers with sacrifices, but the contests and most of the ceremonies were abolished, probably through adversity. The Athenians now celebrated the games on this occasion, adding the novelty of horse-races.

That same winter the Ambraciots marched out against Amphilochian Argos with three thousand heavy infantry, as they had promised Eurylochus when they asked him to keep his army there. They invaded the Argive territory and occupied Olpae, a stronghold on a hill near the sea. The Acarnanians had once fortified it, and the nation used it as its court of assizes. It lies on the coast, about two miles and three-quarters from the city of Argos. The Acarnanians meanwhile sent part of their forces to relieve Argos. With the rest they encamped in Amphilochia at the place called Crenae, or the Wells, to watch for Eurylochus and his Peloponnesians and stop them from passing through to join the Ambraciots. They also sent for Demosthenes, the commander of the Aetolian expedition, to lead them, and for the twenty Athenian ships cruising off Peloponnese under Aristotle, son of Timocrates, and Hierophon, son of Antimnestus. The Ambraciots at Olpae, for their part, sent a messenger to their own city and begged them to come to their aid with their whole levy. They feared that the army of Eurylochus might fail to get through the Acarnanians, and that they would then have to fight alone, or could not retreat, even if they wanted to, without danger.

Eurylochus and his Peloponnesians, meanwhile, learned that the Ambraciots had reached Olpae. They set out in all haste from Proschium to join them. They crossed the Achelous and advanced through Acarnania, which they found empty, since its people had gone to the relief of Argos. On their right they had the city of the Stratians with its garrison, and on their left the rest of Acarnania. They passed through the territory of the Stratians, advanced through Phytia, and, skirting Medeon, through Limnaea. Then they left Acarnania behind and entered a friendly country, that of the Agraeans. From there they reached and crossed Mount Thymaus, which belongs to the Agraeans, and came down into the Argive territory after dark. They passed between the city of Argos and the Acarnanian posts at Crenae, and joined the Ambraciots at Olpae.

At daybreak the two forces united, sat down at the place called Metropolis and encamped. Not long after, the Athenians in the twenty ships entered the Ambracian Gulf to support the Argives, bringing Demosthenes, two hundred Messenian heavy infantry and sixty Athenian archers. While the fleet off Olpae blockaded the hill from the sea, the Acarnanians and a few Amphilochians had already reached Argos. Most of the Amphilochians were held back by force by the Ambraciots. They were making ready to give battle to the enemy, and had chosen Demosthenes to command the whole allied army along with their own generals. Demosthenes led them near Olpae and encamped, a great ravine lying between the two armies. For five days they stayed inactive, and on the sixth both sides drew up in order of battle. The Peloponnesian army was the larger and outflanked its opponents. Demosthenes feared that his right might be surrounded. In a sunken road overgrown with bushes he therefore hid some four hundred heavy infantry and light troops. At the moment of the onset they were to rise behind the enemy’s projecting left wing and attack it in the rear. When both sides were ready, they joined battle. Demosthenes stood on the right wing with the Messenians and a few Athenians. The rest of the line consisted of the different divisions of the Acarnanians and the Amphilochian carters. The Peloponnesians and Ambraciots were drawn up all mixed together, except for the Mantineans, who were massed on the left, though they did not reach the end of the wing. There Eurylochus and his men faced the Messenians and Demosthenes.

The Peloponnesians were well engaged, and their outflanking wing was about to turn the enemy’s right. Then the Acarnanians rose from the ambush, fell on them from behind, and broke them at the first attack, so that they did not even stand to resist. Panic spread, and most of their army fled, terrified beyond measure at the sight of the division of Eurylochus, their best troops, being cut to pieces. Demosthenes and his Messenians, who were posted in this part of the field, did most of the work. Meanwhile the Ambraciots (the best soldiers in those countries) and the troops on the right wing defeated the division facing them and pursued it as far as Argos. On their return from the pursuit they found their main body beaten. The Acarnanians pressed them hard, and they got back to Olpae with difficulty, suffering heavy loss on the way, since they rushed on without discipline or order. Only the Mantineans kept their ranks during the retreat, and better than any others in the army.

The battle lasted until evening. On the next day Menedaius took sole command, since Eurylochus and Macarius were dead. After so signal a defeat he was at a loss. He could not see how to stay and endure a siege, cut off by land and by the Athenian fleet at sea, and he could not see how to retreat safely either. So he opened a parley with Demosthenes and the Acarnanian generals, asking for a truce, permission to retreat, and the recovery of the dead. They gave him the dead, set up a trophy, and took up their own, about three hundred. They publicly refused the army the retreat he asked for. In secret, however, Demosthenes and his Acarnanian colleagues allowed the Mantineans, Menedaius and the other commanders and leading men of the Peloponnesians to leave without delay. Their aim was to strip the Ambraciots and the mercenary host of foreigners of their supporters, and above all to discredit the Lacedaemonians and Peloponnesians with the Hellenes in those parts, as traitors and self-seekers.

The enemy was taking up his dead and burying them in haste as best he could, and those who had obtained permission were secretly planning their retreat. Then word came to Demosthenes and the Acarnanians that the Ambraciots from the city were on the march. They were coming with their whole levy through Amphilochia, in answer to the first message from Olpae, to join their countrymen there, and they knew nothing of what had happened. Demosthenes prepared to march against them with his army. Meanwhile he sent a strong division ahead at once to block the roads and seize the strong positions. In the meantime the Mantineans and the others covered by the agreement went out, pretending to gather herbs and firewood. They slipped away by twos and threes, picking up along the way the things they claimed to have come for. When they had gone some distance from Olpae, they quickened their pace. The Ambraciots and those of the rest who had gone out in larger parties saw them hurrying on. They pushed on in turn and began to run to catch them up. At first the Acarnanians thought that all of them alike were leaving without permission, and began to pursue the Peloponnesians. They believed they were being betrayed, and even threw a dart or two at some of their own generals, who tried to stop them and told them that leave had been granted. In the end, however, they let the Mantineans and Peloponnesians pass and killed only the Ambraciots, though it was hard, and a matter of much dispute, to tell whether a man was an Ambraciot or a Peloponnesian. About two hundred were killed in this way. The rest escaped into the neighboring territory of Agraea and found refuge with Salynthius, the friendly king of the Agraeans.

Meanwhile the Ambraciots from the city reached Idomene. It consists of two lofty hills. The troops Demosthenes had sent ahead took the higher one after nightfall, without being seen by the Ambraciots, who had climbed the smaller and bivouacked below it. After supper, at nightfall, Demosthenes set out with the rest of the army. He himself took half his force toward the pass, and the remainder went by the Amphilochian hills. At dawn he fell on the Ambraciots while they were still in their beds. They knew nothing of what had happened and fully thought the newcomers were their own countrymen. Demosthenes had purposely put the Messenians in front, with orders to speak to them in the Doric dialect and so win the confidence of the sentinels, who could not see them, since it was still dark. So he routed their army the moment he attacked it. Most were killed where they lay, and the rest broke away in flight over the hills. The roads, however, were already occupied. The Amphilochians knew their own country, but the Ambraciots did not and could not tell which way to turn. Their armor was heavy, against a light-armed enemy. So they fell into ravines and into the ambushes laid for them, and perished there. In their many efforts to escape, some even turned to the sea, which was not far away. They saw the Athenian ships coasting along the shore just as the action was going on, and swam out to them. In their panic they thought it better to die, if die they must, at the hands of the Athenians than at those of the barbarous and detested Amphilochians. Of the large Ambraciot force destroyed in this way, only a few reached the city safely. The Acarnanians stripped the dead, set up a trophy, and returned to Argos.

Next day a herald came from the Ambraciots who had fled from Olpae to the Agraeans. He came to ask leave to take up the dead who had fallen after the first engagement, when they left the camp with the Mantineans and their companions, without having, as these had, permission to do so. He saw the arms of the Ambraciots from the city and was astonished at their number. He knew nothing of the disaster and fancied they were the arms of his own party. Someone asked him what astonished him so much and how many of them had been killed. This man in his turn fancied that he was the herald from the troops at Idomene. The herald answered: “About two hundred.” His questioner caught him up, saying: “Why, the arms you see here are those of more than a thousand.” The herald replied: “Then they are not the arms of those who fought with us?” The other answered: “Yes, they are, if at least you fought at Idomene yesterday.” “But we fought no one yesterday; it was the day before, in the retreat.” “However that may be, we fought yesterday against those who came to reinforce you from the city of the Ambraciots.” When the herald heard this and understood that the reinforcement from the city had been destroyed, he broke out in wailing. Stunned by the magnitude of the present evils, he left at once, without performing his errand and without asking again for the dead bodies. This was indeed by far the greatest disaster that befell any one Hellenic city in so few days during this war. I have not set down the number of the dead, because the figure given seems so out of proportion to the size of the city that it is incredible. In any case I know this: if the Acarnanians and Amphilochians had wished to take Ambracia, as the Athenians and Demosthenes advised, they would have taken it without a blow. As it was, they feared that if the Athenians held it, they would be worse neighbors than the present ones.

After this the Acarnanians gave a third of the spoils to the Athenians and divided the rest among their own towns. The Athenians’ share was captured on the voyage home. The arms now deposited in the Attic temples are three hundred panoplies, which the Acarnanians set aside for Demosthenes and which he brought to Athens himself. This exploit made his return home after the Aetolian disaster less dangerous. The Athenians in the twenty ships also went off to Naupactus. When Demosthenes and the Athenians had gone, the Acarnanians and Amphilochians allowed the Ambraciots and Peloponnesians who had taken refuge with Salynthius and the Agraeans to leave freely from Oeniadae, to which they had moved from the country of Salynthius. They also concluded with the Ambraciots a treaty and alliance for one hundred years, on the following terms. It was to be a defensive, not an offensive alliance. The Ambraciots could not be required to march with the Acarnanians against the Peloponnesians, nor the Acarnanians with the Ambraciots against the Athenians. Besides this, the Ambraciots were to give up the places and hostages they held from the Amphilochians, and not to help Anactorium, which was at enmity with the Acarnanians. With this settlement they ended the war. After this the Corinthians sent a garrison of their own citizens to Ambracia: three hundred heavy infantry under Xenocleides, son of Euthycles, who reached their destination after a difficult journey over land. Such was the story of the affair of Ambracia.

That same winter the Athenians in Sicily landed from their ships on the territory of Himera, in concert with the Sicels, who had invaded its borders from the interior, and then sailed to the islands of Aeolus. When they returned to Rhegium, they found that the Athenian general Pythodorus, son of Isolochus, had arrived to take Laches’ place in command of the fleet. The allies in Sicily had sailed to Athens and persuaded the Athenians to send more ships to help them. They pointed out that the Syracusans, who already controlled the land, were working to assemble a navy, so that a few ships should no longer keep them from the sea. The Athenians set about manning forty ships to send to Sicily. They thought the war there would end sooner, and they also wanted to give their navy exercise. One of the generals, Pythodorus, was accordingly sent out with a few ships. Sophocles, son of Sostratides, and Eurymedon, son of Thucles, were to follow with the main body. Meanwhile Pythodorus had taken over Laches’ ships. Toward the end of winter he sailed against the Locrian fort that Laches had taken before, and came back after being beaten in battle by the Locrians.

In the first days of this spring a stream of fire poured out of Etna, as on earlier occasions, and destroyed some land of the Catanians, who live on Mount Etna, the largest mountain in Sicily. Fifty years, it is said, had passed since the last eruption, and there had been three in all since the Hellenes settled Sicily. Such were the events of this winter, and with it ended the sixth year of this war, of which Thucydides was the historian.
